title: Governance at the State Level
summary: India is a federation with governments at the Union and State levels, each with an executive, legislature and judiciary on parliamentary lines. In the State, executive power is vested in the Governor, but the Governor is a nominal head; the real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister.

Appointment: by the President (in practice on the Prime Minister's advice). Qualifications: citizen of India, at least 35 years old, holding no office of profit. Term: five years, but holds office during the pleasure of the President, who may remove him/her earlier. One person may be Governor of two or more States.

Powers: (a) Executive — appoints the Chief Minister (the leader of the majority in the Assembly) and, on the CM's advice, other ministers; appoints the Advocate General, chairpersons and members of the State Public Service Commission, State Election Commission and State Finance Commission, and judges of courts below the High Court; is consulted when the President appoints High Court judges. (b) Legislative — summons and prorogues the legislature and can dissolve the Assembly; addresses it; may nominate one Anglo-Indian to the Assembly and one-sixth of the Legislative Council; a bill becomes law only with the Governor's assent. (c) Financial — the budget is presented on the Governor's behalf; no money bill without the Governor's recommendation; controls the State Contingency Fund. (d) Discretionary — chooses the Chief Minister when no party has a clear majority; may reserve a bill for the President; may report to the President that the State government is not working according to the Constitution, leading to President's Rule under Article 356, when the Governor rules on behalf of the President.

Relationship with the Council of Ministers: normally the Governor acts on its advice and is informed of all its decisions through the Chief Minister; ministers stay in office as long as they enjoy the Assembly's majority. Yet the Governor is not merely ceremonial — he/she becomes effective in political instability, as the link between the Centre and the State, and through discretionary powers.
## Chief Minister and Council of Ministers

The Chief Minister and ministers are appointed by the Governor for five years but stay only while they have majority support; a non-member must become an MLA or MLC within six months. The Chief Minister is the real head of the State government: advises the Governor on appointing ministers and allocates portfolios; presides over and coordinates the Council of Ministers; guides policies and approves bills; is the sole link between the Council of Ministers and the Governor; places a single minister's decision before the whole Council if the Governor wishes. The CM is most powerful with a clear majority; in a coalition government his/her role is limited by partners and independents.

Most States are unicameral (Legislative Assembly only); a few (e.g. Bihar, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) are bicameral with a Legislative Council. The Governor is part of the legislature.

Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha): 60–500 members (smaller in Goa, Sikkim, Mizoram), directly elected by universal adult franchise (all citizens 18 and above); seats reserved for SC and ST. An MLA must be a citizen, 25 years old, on the voters' list, not holding an office of profit or a government job. Term: five years (may be dissolved earlier, or extended by one year at a time in a national emergency).

Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad): not more than one-third of the Assembly's size and not less than 40 (Jammu & Kashmir's had 36). One-third elected by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers and one-sixth nominated by the Governor. It is a permanent house — never dissolved; members serve six years and one-third retire every two years. Minimum age 30. The legislature must meet at least twice a year (gap less than six months).

Functions: (a) Law-making — the Assembly has the final say; the Council can delay an ordinary bill but if the Assembly passes it again it is deemed passed; money bills start only in the Assembly and the Council must return them within 14 days; the Governor cannot refuse assent to a money bill but may return other bills or reserve them for the President. (b) Control over the executive — the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Assembly and can be removed by a no-confidence motion; questions, adjournment motions and calling-attention notices keep a check. (c) Electoral — elected MLAs vote in the election of the President and elect the State's Rajya Sabha members and one-third of the Legislative Council. (d) Constitutional amendments — some need ratification by half the State legislatures.

State governments run welfare schemes: residential bridge courses for out-of-school children in Andhra Pradesh and Rajasthan; hot mid-day meals in over 95,000 primary schools in Uttar Pradesh; Maharashtra's School Sanitation and Hygiene Education programme, where children called 'swachhata doots' spread awareness; and Nagaland's 'communitisation' (from 2002) — sharing management of schools, health and electricity with the community.

Every State has a High Court (one may serve several States — Guwahati High Court serves seven north-eastern States). It has a Chief Justice and judges appointed by the President, who consults the Chief Justice of India (and, for judges, the High Court Chief Justice and the Governor). Qualifications: citizen; 10 years in a judicial office in India, or 10 years as an advocate of a High Court. Judges retire at 65 and can be removed only by impeachment by Parliament for proved misbehaviour or incapacity. Jurisdiction: original (enforcing Fundamental Rights through writs, election petitions) and appellate (appeals from district courts; confirms death sentences); it supervises subordinate courts and is a court of record. Subordinate courts at district level: civil courts (property, contracts, divorce — no punishment), criminal courts (theft, murder — punishment), and revenue courts (Board of Revenue, Commissioner, Collector, Tehsildar).

(1) advises the Governor on the appointment of Council of Ministers and allocation of portfolios to them; presides over the meetings of the State Council of Ministers and also coordinates the functioning of different ministers; (2) The Chief Minister is required to communicate to the Governor all the decisions of the Council of Ministers. is the sole link of communication between the Council of Ministers and the Governor. It is he/she who formulates the policies and guides the Council of Ministers to implement them.
Describe any two legislative powers of a Governor.

(1) He/She addresses the State Legislative Assembly or the joint sessions of the two houses of the legislature. However, the Governor may dissolve the Assembly earlier on the advice of the Chief Minister. (2) He/She also nominates one-sixth of the members to the Legislative Council, if the State has a bi-cameral legislature. A bill passed by the State Legislature becomes a law or Act only when the Governor gives assent to it. He/She can reserve any bill passed by the State Legislature for the consideration of the President of India.

or: Explain any two powers of the Chief Minister of a State.

(2) presides over the meetings of the State Council of Ministers and also coordinates the functioning of different ministers; is the sole link of communication between the Council of Ministers and the Governor. Differentiate between civil cases and criminal cases.

Civil Cases: These cases filed in civil courts pertain to disputes between two or more persons regarding property, breach of agreement or contract, divorce or disputes between landlords and tenants. In such civil cases, the court does not award any punishment as violation of law is not involved. Criminal Cases: Such cases relate to theft, robbery, rape, pick-pocketing, physical murder etc. These cases are filed in the criminal courts by the police, on behalf of the State, against the accused. In such cases, if the court finds the accused guilty, he/she is awarded punishment.
sa: Describe any three executive powers of the Governor of a State.

(1) He/ She appoints the Chief Minister and other members of the Council of Ministers. He appoints only that person as Chief Minister who is the Leader of the majority in the Legislative Assembly. (2) He/She also appoints persons on important posts such as the Chairpersons and Members of the State Public Service Commission, State Election Commission, State Finance Commission and the Advocate General, Judges of the courts, other than the High Court. (3) He/she is consulted on the appointment of High Court judges; all executive action is taken in his/her name, though on the advice of the Council of Ministers.
Explain the executive and legislative powers of the Governor.

(1) At the state level, there is a Governor in whom the executive power of the State is vested by the Constitution. He/ She appoints the Chief Minister and other members of the Council of Ministers. He/She also appoints persons on important posts such as the Chairpersons and Members of the State Public Service Commission, State Election Commission, State Finance Commission and the Advocate General, Judges of the courts, other than the High Court. (2) Legislative: summons and prorogues the legislature and dissolves the Assembly, addresses it, nominates members to the Council (and earlier one Anglo-Indian to the Assembly), and gives assent to bills, returns them or reserves them for the President.
'The Chief Minister is the head of the government in the State and plays a very important role.' Support with examples.

(1) He/she chooses ministers and allocates portfolios (e.g. who handles education or police). (2) presides over the meetings of the State Council of Ministers and also coordinates the functioning of different ministers; It is he/she who formulates the policies and guides the Council of Ministers to implement them. Many times States also adapt Union Governments welfare schemes and implement them. (3) He/she communicates all decisions to the Governor and is praised or blamed for everything that happens in the State; with a clear majority he/she is very powerful, though in a coalition partners limit the role.
Describe the legislative functions of the State Legislature.

(1) A Bill passed by the Legislative Assembly is sent to the Legislative Council which has to pass it or to return it with recommendations to the Legislative Assembly.If the Legislative Assembly passes that Bill once again either with recommendations of the Council or without those, it shall be deemed to have been passed by both the Houses. (2) As regards, Money Bills, these can be introduced only in the Legislative Assembly. After the Assembly passes the Money Bill, it goes to the Legislative Council which has to pass it or return the Bill to the Assembly with its recommendations within 14 days of the receipt of the Bill. (3) He/She cannot withhold the assent on the Money Bill but can send back an ordinary bill for reconsideration or can reserve any of the bills for consideration by the President.

The two houses of the State Legislature are: Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. The members of the Vidhan Sabha also elect the members of the Rajya Sabha from their respective States. Explain the jurisdiction of a High Court.

(1) The High Court exercises original jurisdiction for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights and other legal rights. The High Court may also hear election petitions under its original jurisdiction challenging election of a member of State Legislature. (2) Appellate jurisdiction: hearing appeals against judgments of district judges in civil cases and sessions courts in criminal cases (over seven years' imprisonment); confirming death sentences. (3) High Courts may also punish for contempt or disrespect of the Court. In addition to this, the State Legislative Assembly also controls the Council of Ministers.
la: Explain the powers and position of the Governor of a State.

(1) Executive powers: appoints the Chief Minister and ministers, the Advocate General and heads of State commissions. (2) Legislative powers: summons, prorogues and dissolves the legislature, addresses it, nominates members, and assents to or returns bills or reserves them for the President. (3) In fact, the budget i.e. ‘the Annual Financial Statement’ of the State is prepared and presented by the State Finance Minister before the State Legislature, on behalf Moreover, no money bill can be introduced in the State Legislature without the recommendations of the Governor. He/She also has control over the State Contingency Fund. (4) Discretionary powers: chooses the CM when no party has a majority, reserves bills for the President, and reports for President's Rule under Article 356. (5) But the Governor acts as a nominal head, and the real executive powers are exercised by the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister. Normally, the Governor exercises all his/her powers on the advice of the Council of Ministers. (6) Secondly, the Governor acts as a link between the Centre and the State. be correct to say that the Governor is just a constitutional or ceremonial head. He/ She can exercise his/her powers effectively under certain circumstances, especially when there is political instability in the State. Since he/she is a link between the Centre and the State, he/she becomes very effective, if the central government sends directions to the State government.
Explain the composition of the State Legislature and how it keeps control over the executive.

(1) As we have seen above, the State executive consists of the Governor, the Chief Minister and the Council of Ministers. In most of the States it is unicameral i.e. has only one house. The two houses of the State Legislature are: Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council. (2) The Assembly has 60–500 directly elected members for five years; MLAs must be 25. (3) The Council (not more than one-third of the Assembly, at least 40) is permanent: one-third elected by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-twelfth by graduates, one-twelfth by teachers, one-sixth nominated; members serve six years. Control: (4) Even if the Assembly rejects the recommendations of the Council, it will be deemed to have been passed by both the Houses. The Council of Ministers is responsible to Vidhan Sabha collectively. The Council of Ministers is removed, if the Vidhan Sabha adopts a motion of no-confidence against it. However, a Chief Justice or a Judge can resign. (5) Moreover, The State Legislature keeps checks on the government by asking questions and supplementary questions, moving adjournment motions and calling attention notices. (6) (c) Financial Powers: You must have read in the newspapers that every year the budget is presented by the government in the Legislature for its approval. Moreover, no money bill can be introduced in the State Legislature without the recommendations of the Governor. After the Assembly passes the Money Bill, it goes to the Legislative Council which has to pass it or return the Bill to the Assembly with its recommendations within 14 days of the receipt of the Bill.
